author: Marcus Aurelius
text: very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.
context: A Roman emperor's private notes to himself, never meant for publication.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul
context: People look for retreats in the country or by the sea; Marcus reminds himself the quietest one is within.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The universe is transformation: life is opinion.
context: Two short thoughts Marcus kept close: everything changes, and much of what troubles us is how we see it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,--I am rising to the work of a human being.
context: The emperor talking himself out of bed.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.
context: A central Stoic idea: we cannot always choose what happens, but we can choose how we judge it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like [the wrong-doer].
context: One line on what to do with being wronged.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth.
context: Marcus's cure for a low mood: think of the good in the people around you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
context: A short note on living with difficult people.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee
context: Take life one piece at a time; no single moment is more than you can bear.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong.
context: Marcus on what sets people apart: the ability to love those who hurt us.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
context: The famous opening of Book 2, which goes on to say that none of them can harm you, and we were made to work together.

author: Epictetus
text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
context: The handbook of a former slave turned teacher, compiled by his student Arrian.

author: Epictetus
text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
context: Epictetus on loss: what we love was given to us for a time.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A friend is a person with whom I may be sincere. Before him I may think aloud.
context: From Emerson's essay on the two elements of friendship, truth and tenderness.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: the only way to have a friend is to be one.
context: Emerson's short answer to how friendships are made.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: a friend may well be reckoned the masterpiece of nature.
context: Emerson on the wonder of finding someone who understands you.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
context: From Emerson's best-known essay, on trusting your own convictions.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
context: The closing lines of "Self-Reliance".

author: Henry David Thoreau
reference: Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (1854)
text: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
context: Thoreau on why he spent two years in a cabin by Walden Pond.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Only that day dawns to which we are awake. There is more day to dawn. The sun is but a morning star.
context: The last lines of Walden.

author: Thomas à Kempis
reference: The Imitation of Christ, Book 3, Chapter 5
text: love feeleth no burden, reckoneth not labours, striveth after more than it is able to do
context: A fifteenth-century devotional classic, on what love makes possible.

author: Thomas à Kempis
reference: The Imitation of Christ, Book 2, Chapter 10
text: Be thankful, therefore, for the least benefit and thou shalt be worthy to receive greater.
context: On gratitude for small things.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
context: The first paragraph of Augustine's account of his life and search for God.

author: Boethius
reference: The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, Prose 4
text: nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
context: Written in prison awaiting execution, as a conversation with Lady Philosophy.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: Hope is the thing with feathers That perches in the soul, And sings the tune without the words, And never stops at all
context: One of Dickinson's best-loved poems. Almost none of her poems were published until after her death.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: If I can stop one heart from breaking, I shall not live in vain;
context: A short poem on what makes a life worthwhile: easing even one person's pain.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: A word is dead When it is said, Some say. I say it just Begins to live That day.
context: The whole of a tiny poem about why words matter after they are spoken.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: We never know how high we are Till we are called to rise; And then, if we are true to plan, Our statures touch the skies.
context: Dickinson on how people find out what they can do only when they are asked to do it.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: Not knowing when the dawn will come I open every door;
context: The opening of a short poem about waiting for good things with every door open.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: There is no frigate like a book To take us lands away,
context: Dickinson on reading as the cheapest way to travel.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: I stepped from plank to plank So slow and cautiously; The stars about my head I felt, About my feet the sea.
context: A poem about getting through an uncertain time one careful step at a time.

author: Emily Dickinson
text: The pedigree of honey Does not concern the bee; A clover, any time, to him Is aristocracy.
context: A playful poem: the bee does not care where the flower came from, only that it is sweet.

author: Christina Rossetti
text: My heart is like a singing bird Whose nest is in a watered shoot; My heart is like an apple-tree Whose boughs are bent with thick-set fruit;
context: The opening of Rossetti's poem "A Birthday", about a heart too glad to hold still.

author: Christina Rossetti
text: there is no friend like a sister, In calm or stormy weather, To cheer one on the tedious way, To fetch one if one goes astray, To lift one if one totters down, To strengthen whilst one stands.
context: The closing lines of "Goblin Market", where one sister has risked everything to save the other.

author: Christina Rossetti
text: Better by far you should forget and smile Than that you should remember and be sad.
context: The end of Rossetti's sonnet in which someone who has died wants those left behind to be happy.

author: Christina Rossetti
text: If I were a Queen, What would I do? I’d make you King, And I’d wait on you.
context: A nursery rhyme from Rossetti's book of poems for children.

author: Christina Rossetti
text: A diamond is a brilliant stone, To catch the world’s desire; An opal holds a fiery spark; But a flint holds fire.
context: A children's rhyme with a quiet point: the plain stone is the one that can make fire.

author: Jane Austen
text: There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises with every attempt to intimidate me.
context: Elizabeth Bennet, teasing Mr. Darcy, who has come to listen to her play the piano.

author: Jane Austen
text: Think only of the past as its remembrance gives you pleasure.
context: Elizabeth tells Darcy to let go of their old misunderstandings and keep only the good memories.

author: Jane Austen
text: I declare, after all, there is no enjoyment like reading! How much sooner one tires of anything than of a book!
context: Caroline Bingley says this with a yawn, pretending to read to impress Mr. Darcy. Austen is laughing, but the line stands.

author: Jane Austen
text: Oh, why is not everybody as happy?
context: Jane Bennet, just engaged, can hardly believe her own happiness.

author: Jane Austen
text: One half of the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other.
context: Emma, cheerfully explaining to her father why other people enjoy things he cannot see the point of.

author: Jane Austen
text: Business, you know, may bring money, but friendship hardly ever does.
context: John Knightley, dryly, to a young woman who walks to the post office every day for letters from friends.

author: Jane Austen
text: silly things do cease to be silly if they are done by sensible people in an impudent way.
context: Emma decides that Frank Churchill's spur-of-the-moment trip to London for a haircut was charming after all.

author: Jane Austen
text: Where shall we see a better daughter, or a kinder sister, or a truer friend?
context: Mrs. Weston, defending Emma warmly to Mr. Knightley.

author: Jane Austen
text: Nobody cares for a letter; the thing is, to be always happy with pleasant companions.
context: Harriet Smith's simple philosophy of life, offered with complete sincerity.

author: Jane Austen
text: You must be the best judge of your own happiness.
context: Emma to her friend Harriet, who is deciding whether to accept a proposal. Emma has her own hopes for the answer, but the advice is sound.

author: Jane Austen
text: My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people, who have a great deal of conversation; that is what I call good company.
context: Anne Elliot, gently disagreeing with a cousin who values rank over conversation.

author: Jane Austen
text: Let those who would be happy be firm.
context: Captain Wentworth, admiring someone who knows her own mind.

author: Jane Austen
text: I wish as well as every body else to be perfectly happy; but, like every body else it must be in my own way.
context: Edward Ferrars, explaining that he has no wish for the grand career his family wants for him.

author: Jane Austen
text: Know your own happiness.
context: Mrs. Dashwood's advice to a young man who cannot see how much he has.

author: Jane Austen
text: We have all a better guide in ourselves, if we would attend to it, than any other person can be.
context: Fanny Price refuses to be anyone's rule of right, and points them back to their own conscience.

author: Jane Austen
text: Selfishness must always be forgiven, you know, because there is no hope of a cure.
context: Mary Crawford, cheerfully apologising for keeping a borrowed horse too long.

author: Jane Austen
text: There will be little rubs and disappointments everywhere, and we are all apt to expect too much; but then, if one scheme of happiness fails, human nature turns to another;
context: Mrs. Grant's practical comfort: when one plan fails, people find another way to be happy.

author: Jane Austen
text: The person, be it gentleman or lady, who has not pleasure in a good novel, must be intolerably stupid.
context: Henry Tilney, happily admitting he loves the same novels Catherine does.

author: Jane Austen
text: Friendship is certainly the finest balm for the pangs of disappointed love.
context: Austen's narrator, on how a new friend helps when a hoped-for romance has not appeared.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m not afraid of storms, for I’m learning how to sail my ship.
context: Amy, newly married, on facing whatever comes.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I like good strong words that mean something,
context: Jo March, defending her colourful language on a cold, windy walk.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Have regular hours for work and play, make each day both useful and pleasant,
context: Mrs. March, after her daughters try a week of doing nothing at all and hate it.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Be comforted, dear soul! There is always light behind the clouds.
context: What the moon seems to whisper to Meg on the night bad news arrives about their father.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: let us be elegant or die.
context: The March sisters, in tight shoes and too many hairpins, heading to a New Year's Eve dance.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: though they seem heavy sometimes, they are good for us, and lighten as we learn to carry them.
context: Mrs. March on everyday responsibilities: they get lighter as we get used to carrying them.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’d rather take coffee than compliments just now.
context: Amy, briskly ordering Laurie to stop flattering her and pour the coffee.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: love is the only thing that we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the end so easy.
context: Beth, near the end of her life, comforting her sister Jo.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I hate to think I’ve got to grow up, and be Miss March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China Aster!
context: Jo March at fifteen, shaking her hair loose in protest at being a young lady.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: love is a great beautifier.
context: On Meg, engaged and prettier than ever.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Rich or poor, we will keep together and be happy in one another.
context: The March parents, refusing a rich relative's offer to take one of their daughters off their hands.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Everyone is very kind, and we are as happy as we can be without you.
context: From the sisters' letters to their mother while she is away nursing their father.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Hope and keep busy,
context: Mrs. March's advice to her daughters as she leaves to care for their wounded father.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m glad you began at once, and hope you will keep on.
context: Mrs. March, pleased to see her daughters start on a good resolution straight away.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: it’s so comfortable to say all I think to you, and feel so safe and happy here.
context: Jo, talking late at night with her mother after a hard day.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: We used to have such happy times, and it's so pleasant to think about them now.
context: Polly, remembering the little brother she lost, with gladness rather than only sorrow.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Well, if I can't be happy, I can be useful, perhaps.
context: Polly, on a lonely day, deciding to do some good instead of moping.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: keep yourself happy, if you can; it will help other people to see you cheerful.
context: Polly's advice to a friend who is bored and low.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: So clever, and energetic, and kind, and happy, it always does me good to see them,
context: Polly, full of admiration for a group of hard-working young women.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: It adds so much to one's happiness to love the task one does.
context: Meg, glad that her son has found work he loves, and remembering how she once hated teaching.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I have fumbled my way into my right place at last, I hope.
context: Demi, after trying several jobs, settles into one that fits.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: We all wish you well and hope much for you.
context: Jo's send-off to Nat as he leaves to study music abroad.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I think you have the courage, and this proves that you have perseverance.
context: A great actress, encouraging a young woman who wants to go on the stage.

author: Louisa May Alcott
reference: Work: A Story of Experience, Chapter 5 (1873)
text: This day is to be a happy one, no matter what comes after it.
context: Helen, who is very ill, decides that this one day with her brothers will be a happy one.

author: Louisa May Alcott
reference: Work: A Story of Experience, Chapter 1 (1873)
text: I want work that I can put my heart into, and feel that it does me good, no matter how hard it is.
context: Christie, at twenty-one, leaving home to make her own way.

author: Louisa May Alcott
reference: Work: A Story of Experience, Chapter 6 (1873)
text: Will you be my friend, and let me be yours?
context: Christie, reaching out to a lonely new acquaintance.

author: Louisa May Alcott
reference: Work: A Story of Experience, Chapter 4 (1873)
text: She seldom wept, but when any thing did unseal the fountains that lay so deep, she cried with all her heart, and felt the better for it.
context: On Christie, who rarely cried, and found that a good cry helped.

author: Helen Keller
text: although the world is full of suffering, it is full also of the overcoming of it.
context: Written while Keller was a student at Radcliffe, the first deafblind person to earn a college degree.

author: Helen Keller
text: Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement; nothing can be done without hope.
context: Keller on hope as the starting point of everything people have built.

author: Helen Keller
text: Once I knew only darkness and stillness. Now I know hope and joy.
context: Keller looking back on her early childhood, before her teacher came.

author: Helen Keller
text: I tried again with new courage and succeeded almost before I knew it.
context: Keller on returning to a task she had been stuck on, after a cheerful essay lifted her mood.

author: Helen Keller
text: The world is sown with good; but unless I turn my glad thoughts into practical living and till my own field, I cannot reap a kernel of the good.
context: Keller on optimism as something you do, not only something you feel.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Part 3, her address at Mt. Airy (1896)
text: One can never consent to creep when one feels an impulse to soar.
context: From a speech Keller gave at sixteen, about learning to speak aloud when many thought she never could.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Chapter 22 (1903)
text: Everything has its wonders, even darkness and silence, and I learn, whatever state I may be in, therein to be content.
context: Keller, who could neither see nor hear, on finding wonder in her own world.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Chapter 23 (1903)
text: my friends have made the story of my life. In a thousand ways they have turned my limitations into beautiful privileges,
context: The closing thanks of Keller's autobiography, written when she was twenty-two.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Chapter 20 (1903)
text: I slip back many times, I fall, I stand still, I run against the edge of hidden obstacles, I lose my temper and find it again and keep it better, I trudge on, I gain a little,
context: Keller on the slow, uneven climb of her college studies.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Chapter 6 (1903)
text: You cannot touch love either; but you feel the sweetness that it pours into everything.
context: Her teacher Anne Sullivan, explaining to young Helen what the word love means.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Chapter 6 (1903)
text: I felt that there were invisible lines stretched between my spirit and the spirits of others.
context: Keller remembering the moment she first understood love.

author: Helen Keller
reference: The Story of My Life, Chapter 7 (1903)
text: there is not a talent, or an aspiration or a joy in me that has not been awakened by her loving touch.
context: Keller on her teacher, Anne Sullivan.

author: Seneca
reference: Minor Dialogues, "On the Shortness of Life", 1
text: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry out the most important projects:
context: The opening argument of Seneca's essay: life is not short, we just let it slip away.

author: Seneca
text: Fire tries gold, misfortune tries brave men.
context: Seneca on why hard times show what people are made of.

author: Seneca
text: He who receives a benefit with gratitude, repays the first instalment of it.
context: Seneca's long essay on giving and receiving kindness: thanking someone well is already a way of repaying them.

author: Seneca
text: It is not, therefore, the thing which is done or given, but the spirit in which it is done or given, that must be considered,
context: Seneca on what makes a gift a gift: the care behind it, not its price.

author: Epictetus
text: All great things are slow of growth; nay, this is true even of a grape or of a fig.
context: Epictetus to a man hoping to make peace with his brother: good things take time to ripen.

author: Epictetus
text: Try to enjoy the great festival of life with other men.
context: One of the shortest of the sayings his students wrote down.

author: Epictetus
text: If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write.
context: Epictetus on habits: we become what we practise.

author: Epictetus
text: I used to be in passion every day; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth.
context: Epictetus on breaking a bad temper slowly: count the good days, and let progress be gradual.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm.
context: From Emerson's essay on how every life keeps drawing new and larger circles.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Happy is the house that shelters a friend!
context: Emerson on the joy of having a friend under your roof.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I awoke this morning with devout thanksgiving for my friends, the old and the new.
context: Emerson, waking up grateful for the people in his life.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Insist on yourself; never imitate.
context: Emerson on trusting your own gifts instead of borrowing someone else's.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think.
context: Emerson on doing what you know is right, whatever others say.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The years teach much which the days never know.
context: Emerson on how the meaning of a life shows only over time.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Rings and other jewels are not gifts, but apologies for gifts. The only gift is a portion of thyself.
context: Emerson's short essay on giving: the best present is something of yourself.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The ornament of a house is the friends who frequent it.
context: Emerson on what really makes a home beautiful.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year.
context: Emerson on not waiting for some better day to come along.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Hitch your wagon to a star.
context: Emerson's famous advice to aim high and let great things pull you along.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
reference: The Conduct of Life, "Considerations by the Way" (1860)
text: Our chief want in life, is, somebody who shall make us do what we can. This is the service of a friend.
context: Emerson on what a real friend does: brings out the best we are capable of.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.
context: What Thoreau says he learned from his two years at Walden Pond.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them.
context: Thoreau's cheerful defence of big dreams, as long as you then build on them.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society.
context: Thoreau, in his one-room cabin, on how he made room for visitors.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I have a great deal of company in my house; especially in the morning, when nobody calls.
context: Thoreau, poking fun at the idea that living alone must be lonely.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Not till we are lost, in other words not till we have lost the world, do we begin to find ourselves,
context: Thoreau on getting lost in the woods at night, and what it teaches.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away.
context: Thoreau on going at your own pace, in your own direction.

author: Henry David Thoreau
work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
reference: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, "Wednesday" (1849)
text: The language of Friendship is not words, but meanings.
context: From a long passage on friendship in Thoreau's first book, about a boat trip with his brother.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Every child begins the world again, to some extent, and loves to stay out doors, even in wet and cold.
context: Thoreau on children, who rediscover the world for themselves.

author: Walt Whitman
text: I celebrate myself, and sing myself,
context: The first line of Whitman's best-known poem.

author: Walt Whitman
text: Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)
context: Whitman, cheerfully unbothered by being more than one thing.

author: Walt Whitman
reference: Leaves of Grass, "Song of the Open Road", 1
text: Afoot and light-hearted I take to the open road, Healthy, free, the world before me, The long brown path before me leading wherever I choose.
context: The opening of Whitman's poem about setting out.

author: Walt Whitman
reference: Leaves of Grass, "Song of the Open Road", 1
text: Henceforth I ask not good-fortune, I myself am good-fortune,
context: Whitman, starting out on the road and deciding to make his own luck.

author: Walt Whitman
text: I exist as I am, that is enough,
context: Whitman on not needing anyone's approval to be who you are.

author: Walt Whitman
text: Failing to fetch me at first keep encouraged, Missing me one place search another, I stop somewhere waiting for you.
context: The last lines of "Song of Myself", where the poet promises he is never far away.

author: Walt Whitman
reference: Leaves of Grass, "I Sing the Body Electric", 4
text: I have perceiv’d that to be with those I like is enough,
context: Whitman on the simple happiness of good company.

author: Walt Whitman
reference: Leaves of Grass, "A Song for Occupations", 6
text: Happiness, knowledge, not in another place but this place, not for another hour but this hour,
context: Whitman on finding happiness right where you are.

author: Walt Whitman
text: It is not upon you alone the dark patches fall, The dark threw its patches down upon me also,
context: Whitman, speaking to future readers: whatever weighs on you, he felt it too.

author: William Shakespeare
reference: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 3, Scene 2
text: And though she be but little, she is fierce.
context: Helena, in the middle of a quarrel, on her small but formidable friend Hermia.

author: William Shakespeare
reference: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 1, Scene 1
text: The course of true love never did run smooth.
context: Lysander, consoling Hermia when their families stand in the way.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Our doubts are traitors, And make us lose the good we oft might win By fearing to attempt.
context: Lucio, urging Isabella to try, even though she doubts she can help.

author: William Shakespeare
text: what’s past is prologue
context: Four words from The Tempest: everything so far has only set the stage.

author: William Shakespeare
text: we know what we are, but know not what we may be.
context: One of Ophelia's lines in Hamlet, which has outlived its scene.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Give sorrow words.
context: Malcolm, to a friend who has just heard terrible news: talk about it, do not hold it in.

author: William Shakespeare
reference: Much Ado About Nothing, Act 3, Scene 2
text: everyone can master a grief but he that has it.
context: Benedick, on how easy it is to give advice about pain that is not your own.

author: William Shakespeare
reference: The Merchant of Venice, Act 1, Scene 1
text: With mirth and laughter let old wrinkles come,
context: Gratiano, cheering up a gloomy friend: if we are going to age, let it be from laughing.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon ’em.
context: From a prank letter in Twelfth Night, now a line people use in earnest.

author: William Shakespeare
reference: All's Well That Ends Well, Act 1, Scene 1
text: Love all, trust a few, Do wrong to none.
context: A mother's advice to her son as he leaves home.

author: William Shakespeare
text: a light heart lives long.
context: A friend's teasing wish in Love's Labour's Lost.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I would not wish Any companion in the world but you;
context: Miranda, speaking to Ferdinand.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Let me not to the marriage of true minds Admit impediments,
context: The opening of the sonnet most often read at weddings.

author: William Shakespeare
text: But if the while I think on thee (dear friend) All losses are restored, and sorrows end.
context: The end of a sonnet about old sorrows, and the one thought that undoes them.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I count myself in nothing else so happy As in a soul rememb’ring my good friends;
context: Bolingbroke, thanking a young ally for his loyalty.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I can no other answer make but thanks, And thanks, and ever thanks;
context: Sebastian, to the friend who followed him into a strange city to keep him safe.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Come what come may, Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.
context: Even the hardest day comes to an end.

author: William Shakespeare
text: A merry heart goes all the day, Your sad tires in a mile-a.
context: A walking song sung by Autolycus, a cheerful rogue.

author: William Shakespeare
text: joy’s soul lies in the doing.
context: Cressida: the real pleasure is in the doing, not the having done.

author: Lao Tzu
text: the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
context: The source of a famous saying. A li is an old Chinese measure of distance, about a third of a mile.

author: Lao Tzu
text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout;
context: Lao Tzu on how everything great starts small.

author: Lao Tzu
text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.
context: One of the best-known passages of the Tao Teh King, a short book of Chinese wisdom from about 2,500 years ago.

author: Lao Tzu
text: He who is satisfied with his lot is rich;
context: Lao Tzu on contentment as a kind of wealth.

author: Lao Tzu
text: The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.
context: A favourite idea of Lao Tzu's: gentleness, like water, wears down what is hard.

author: Confucius
text: Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?
context: From the very first passage of the Analects, the sayings of Confucius gathered by his students.

author: Confucius
text: When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
context: Confucius on how hard times show who and what lasts.

author: Confucius
text: Virtue is not left to stand alone. He who practises it will have neighbors.
context: Confucius on how goodness draws good people near.

author: Confucius
text: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
context: Confucius on the difference between knowing something, loving it and delighting in it.

author: Confucius
text: The wise are free from perplexities; the virtuous from anxiety; and the bold from fear.
context: Three short lines on what wisdom, goodness and courage each give us.

author: Confucius
text: The days and months are passing away; the years do not wait for us.
context: Said to Confucius to urge him to take up public work while he still could. He agreed.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: If you shed tears when you miss the sun, you also miss the stars.
context: From Tagore's book of short sayings, which he wrote in English himself.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: Let life be beautiful like summer flowers and death like autumn leaves.
context: One of Tagore's short sayings, comparing a good life and a gentle end to the seasons.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: You smiled and talked to me of nothing and I felt that for this I had been waiting long.
context: Tagore on the quiet happiness of easy conversation with someone you love.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: Let me think that there is one among those stars that guides my life through the dark unknown.
context: A short saying about finding something to steer by in uncertain times.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: Do not say, "It is morning," and dismiss it with a name of yesterday. See it for the first time as a new-born child that has no name.
context: Tagore on meeting each day as if it were brand new.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: The roots below the earth claim no rewards for making the branches fruitful.
context: Tagore on the people whose quiet support makes everything else possible.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: Thank the flame for its light, but do not forget the lampholder standing in the shade with constancy of patience.
context: A saying about remembering those who help without being seen.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: Rest belongs to the work as the eyelids to the eyes.
context: Tagore on rest as part of the work, not a break from it.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: We live in this world when we love it.
context: One of the shortest of Tagore's sayings.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: The waterfall sings, "I find my song, when I find my freedom."
context: Tagore on how people come into their own when they are free to.
